sampling-distributions-s1.title: Simulated sample means of wait times
sampling-distributions-s1.text: Wait times at a pharmacy counter are strongly skewed right, with mean 5 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. A computer took 200 random samples of 5 customers and 200 random samples of 40 customers and found the mean wait time of each sample. The boxplots show the 200 sample means for each sample size (simulated data).

plot.label: Boxplots of 200 simulated sample means of wait time for samples of 5 customers and of 40 customers; both centered near 5 minutes, the n = 40 means much less spread out

sampling-distributions-s2.title: Simulated sample proportions
sampling-distributions-s2.text: In a large city, 40% of voters support a new park tax. A computer took 500 random samples of 100 voters each and found the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ of supporters in each sample. The histogram shows the 500 values of $\hat{p}$ (simulated data).

plot.label: Histogram of 500 simulated sample proportions from samples of 100 voters, centered near 0.40 and roughly symmetric, from about 0.24 to 0.56

items.q: How do the centers of the two distributions of sample means compare?

why.correct: Both are centered near 5 minutes (medians 4.32 and 4.84; means 4.91 and 5.01), the population mean: the mean of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is $\mu$, whatever the sample size.
options: A larger sample does not move the center; it shrinks the spread.
Sample means are centered at the population mean, 5 minutes.
Right: $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$ for any sample size.
The sample size sets the spread, not the center.
The n = 40 means are centered much higher, because larger samples catch more long waits
The n = 5 means are centered near 1 minute, the most common single wait
Both are centered near 5 minutes, the population mean
The n = 40 means are centered near 40 minutes, the sample size

why.correct: The means of samples of 40 vary much less (SD about 0.84 minutes) than the means of samples of 5 (about 2.4). The formula $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ gives $\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 2.24$ and $\frac{5}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.79$.
options: More customers per sample average out more, so the means vary less.
The number of samples does not set the spread; the sample size does.
Averages of 5 values still vary from sample to sample.
Right: larger samples give less variable sample means.
The n = 40 means are more spread out, because there are more customers in each sample
The spreads are about the same, because both used 200 samples
The n = 5 means have no spread, because each is an average
The n = 40 means are much less spread out than the n = 5 means

items.q: What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ for samples of 40 customers, in minutes?

mistakes.why: Divide by the square root of n, not by n.
That is the standard deviation of single wait times, the population. Means of 40 vary much less.

items.q: The population of wait times is strongly skewed right. What about the shapes of the two distributions of sample means?

why.correct: With n = 5 the sample means are still skewed right, with high outliers. With n = 40 they are close to symmetric: by the Central Limit Theorem, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal when n is large.
options: The skew fades as n grows; with n = 40 the means are close to symmetric.
Right: the Central Limit Theorem at work as n grows.
Means of small samples from a skewed population keep some skew.
It is the other way around: more averaging means less skew.
Both are skewed right, since the population is skewed right
n = 5: still skewed right; n = 40: close to symmetric
Both are exactly normal, since they are made of means
The n = 5 means are symmetric and the n = 40 means are skewed

items.q: One random sample of 40 customers has a mean wait of 7.5 minutes. Based on the sampling distribution, is that surprising?

why.correct: For n = 40, $\bar{x}$ is approximately $N\left(5, \frac{5}{\sqrt{40}}\right)$, so 7.5 is $\frac{7.5 - 5}{0.79} \approx 3.2$ standard deviations above the center. That would be very unusual if the pharmacy's waits were as described.
options: Single waits are common there, but a mean of 40 waits that high is not.
Means vary, but values far from 5 minutes are rare for n = 40.
Right: sample means of 40 rarely land that far out.
Many sample means are above 5; what matters is how far, in SDs of $\bar{x}$.
No: single waits of 7.5 minutes are common in a skewed population
No: sample means vary, so any value is equally likely
Yes: it is more than 3 standard deviations of $\bar{x}$ above 5 minutes
Yes, and the reason is simply that 7.5 is more than the mean of 5 minutes

items.q: What does one of the 500 values in the histogram represent?

why.correct: Each value is a statistic: the proportion of supporters in one random sample of 100 voters.
options: One voter gives a yes or no; a sample of 100 gives a proportion.
That is the parameter, one fixed number.
The bar heights count samples; each value is a proportion.
Right: one sample, one $\hat{p}$.
The opinion of one voter, support or not, in a single sample
The proportion of supporters among the city's voters, 0.40
The number of samples that had 40 supporters out of 100
The proportion of supporters in one random sample of 100 voters

items.q: Where is the distribution of $\hat{p}$ centered, and why?

why.correct: The values are centered near 0.40 (their mean is about 0.401), the population proportion: the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is centered at p.
options: Right: $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$.
Two possible answers do not make each one half as likely.
The values are proportions between 0 and 1.
0.60 is the other group; the histogram shows supporters.
Near 0.40, the proportion of all the city's voters who support the tax
Near 0.50, since voters either support the tax or they do not
Near 100, the number of voters in each sample
Near 0.60, the proportion of voters who do not support it

items.q: If the computer had taken samples of 400 voters instead of 100, how would the histogram change?

why.correct: Same center, 0.40, but less spread: four times the sample size cuts the spread of $\hat{p}$ in half, from about 0.049 to about 0.024. Larger random samples give statistics closer to the parameter.
options: More voters per sample make $\hat{p}$ less variable, not more.
Right: spread shrinks like $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, and $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
The center stays at the population proportion, 0.40.
The population is the same, but the sample size changes the spread.
Same center, but four times as spread out
Same center, but about half as spread out
The center would move from 0.40 to 0.10
It would not change, since the city has the same voters

items.q: In this setting, which is a parameter and which is a statistic?

why.correct: A parameter describes the population (0.40 of all the city's voters). A statistic describes a sample ($\hat{p}$ for each sample of 100), and it varies from sample to sample.
options: That is reversed: the 0.40 describes every voter in the city.
Being a proportion does not decide it; population or sample does.
Right: population number, then sample numbers.
Each $\hat{p}$ describes only its own sample of 100.
0.40 is a statistic; each $\hat{p}$ is a parameter
Both are statistics, since both are proportions
0.40 is a parameter; each $\hat{p}$ is a statistic
Both are parameters, since they describe the same voters

items.q: What is the sampling distribution of a statistic?

why.correct: The sampling distribution is the distribution of the values a statistic takes in all possible random samples of the same size from the same population.
options: That is the distribution of a sample, not of a statistic.
That is the population distribution.
Sampling methods are a design choice, not a distribution.
Right: it shows how the statistic varies from sample to sample.
The distribution of the data values in one random sample
The distribution of the values in the whole population
The list of sampling methods, such as stratified or cluster, a study could use
The distribution of its values in all possible random samples of the same size

items.q: Which statement is the Central Limit Theorem?

why.correct: The CLT is about sample means: when n is large, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population. A common guide is n of 30 or more.
options: Right: the shape of $\bar{x}$, not of the data.
A sample from a skewed population stays skewed, however large.
Sampling does not change the population.
The sample mean still varies; it just varies less.
For large n, $\bar{x}$ has an approximately normal sampling distribution
When n is large, the data values in one sample are approximately normal in shape
When n is large, the population becomes approximately normal
When n is large, the sample mean equals the population mean

items.q: The weights of a breed of cats are approximately normal. What is the shape of the sampling distribution of the mean weight for random samples of 5 cats?

why.correct: If the population is normal, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is normal for any sample size. The Central Limit Theorem is needed only when the population is not normal.
options: The 30 guide matters for a non-normal population. This one is normal.
Right: normal in, normal out, at any n.
Random selection does not make the means uniform.
A normal population already settles it.
Skewed, because 5 is less than 30
Normal, because the population is normal
Uniform, because each cat is equally likely to be chosen
Impossible to say without a sample of 30 or more cats

items.q: Pharmacy wait times have mean 5 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes (skewed right). For a random sample of 40 customers, what is the probability that the sample mean wait is more than 6 minutes?

why.correct: With n = 40, the CLT makes $\bar{x}$ approximately $N\left(5, \frac{5}{\sqrt{40}}\right) = N(5, 0.791)$. $z = \frac{6 - 5}{0.791} \approx 1.26$, so $P(\bar{x} > 6) \approx 0.103$.

mistakes.why: That uses $\sigma = 5$, the spread of single waits. A mean of 40 waits has $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{40}}$.
That is the area below 6 minutes. "More than" is the right tail.

items.q: A researcher measures the heights of 50 randomly chosen sunflowers in a field of 10,000 and finds their mean. Which describes the sampling distribution in this study?

why.correct: Three distributions: the population (all 10,000 heights), the sample (the 50 heights), and the sampling distribution (the means of every possible sample of 50).
options: That is the sample's distribution.
That is the population's distribution.
One value is one point in the sampling distribution.
Right: the values of the statistic over all samples.
The distribution of the 50 sunflower heights that the researcher measured in the field
The distribution of the heights of the 10,000 sunflowers
The single mean height that the researcher computed
The mean heights from every possible random sample of 50 sunflowers

items.q: A survey firm wants its sample means to vary half as much from sample to sample. How should it change its sample size?

why.correct: The spread of $\bar{x}$ is $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. To halve it, $\sqrt{n}$ must double, so n must be 4 times as large.
options: Right: $\sqrt{4n} = 2\sqrt{n}$.
Doubling n divides the spread by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$, not by 2.
A smaller sample makes the means vary more.
The number of samples does not change how much each sample mean varies.
Use a sample 4 times as large
Use a sample 2 times as large
Use a sample half as large
Keep the sample size and take twice as many samples

items.q: The pharmacy says its waits have mean 5 minutes and SD 5 minutes. A random sample of 40 customers had a mean wait of 7.5 minutes. If the pharmacy is right, $P(\bar{x} \ge 7.5) \approx 0.0008$ (z about 3.16). Build a conclusion about the pharmacy's statement.

why.correct: The probability is computed assuming the pharmacy's numbers. A sample mean this high would almost never happen by chance, so the sample casts doubt on the statement.

evidence.label: Probability
options: If the mean wait is 5 minutes, a sample mean of 7.5 or more for 40 customers has probability about 0.0008
The probability that the mean wait is 5 minutes is about 0.0008
About 0.08% of single customers wait 7.5 minutes or more

why.1: The probability assumes the pharmacy's mean; it is not the chance the mean is 5.
why.2: It is about sample means of 40, not single waits.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: so the sample gives strong reason to doubt that the mean wait is 5 minutes
so the mean wait is shown to be exactly 7.5 minutes
so the sample is typical of a mean wait of 5 minutes

why.1: One sample does not pin the mean down exactly.
why.2: A result more than 3 SDs out is not typical.

conclude.model: If the pharmacy's mean wait were 5 minutes, a random sample of 40 customers would have a mean wait of 7.5 minutes or more with probability only about 0.0008. Because that is so unlikely, the sample gives strong reason to doubt that the mean wait is 5 minutes.
